transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-28 15:30 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Samir Huang (Redwood), Alex Nwosu (Argon), Priya Menon (Argon), Diego Ramos (Argon)

Auto-summary (may be imperfect): triage of kernel switching pathologies on on-prem; discussed cuda graph replay flakiness when KV cache is warm, how batching pipeline interacts with quantized kernels, and how VPC egress rules increase p99.

Transcript body:
[00:00:02] Maya: okay hey everyone thanks for jumping on, um we'll kick off, Jordan is gonna lead the deep dive on the kernel switching traces, I think Alex sent some logs, right?
[00:00:12] Alex: yeah we dumped a couple of nsight captures and a handful of kernel time series. sorry if some of the file names are weird i put them in the shared drive, link in the calendar notes.
[00:00:25] Jordan: cool thanks, i pulled the traces, and the interesting bit is not just a single kernel slowdown it's a handoff sequence — we see TRT-llm kernels then a dynamic vllm path kicking in, then cuda-graph replay aborts and a small stall while falling back.
[00:00:40] Priya: mmhmm, that's what we noticed in production, bursts cause tail latency spikes, p99 jumps by ~300ms and sometimes requests timeout at the app layer.
[00:00:50] Samir: quick disclaimer, some names in the traces are auto-symbolized wrong so "Tensorrt llm" shows up as two entries, ignore that mapping error.
[00:01:02] Diego: security side — we also saw that under VPC egress pinned routes the retransmit and ARP noise increases, could that tie into kernel scheduling?
[00:01:12] Jordan: potentially, there's two coupling points: the NIC driver jitter affects DMA timing, which can shift CUDA stream timing and lead to different kernel launch heuristics. But more concretely we saw KV cache thrash: when many short prefix hits arrive, the runtime's prefix caching sets a path that assumes small batch sizes, then a sudden large request forces a different kernel layout. The kernel router then switches exec paths.
[00:01:37] Alex: when you say "router" you mean Redwood runtime? our team calls it the execpath tiebreaker uh policy.
[00:01:45] Jordan: yes, right, the runtime decides based on sequence length, quantization, and batch composition. In your traces, sequence distribution was bimodal which confuses the kernel mapper.
[00:01:57] Priya: can you explain the cuda graph replay failure more simply? we saw occasional "replay mismatch" logs and then the system falls back to non-graph launches.
[00:02:06] Jordan: sure — during warmup we capture a cuda graph for a common path and replay it; it's very fast. But if the next request deviates from the captured shape (e.g. kv cache present or absent) replay can fail with a runtime check. The recovery path involves tearing down the graph and relaunching individual kernels which spikes latency.
[00:02:25] Maya: and empirically Argon saw that happen mostly during bursty traffic windows?
[00:02:30] Alex: yes, mostly when our front-end bursts after a cache flush, and when quantization mode toggles between requests.
[00:02:36] Jordan: the quantization toggle bit is important — TRT-LLM quantized int4 kernels have different memory layout and prefetch patterns than vLLM fp16. When the runtime swaps kernel types midstream we can get memory bank contention and extra copies.
[00:02:50] Diego: is there any often-missed interaction with NUMA or NVLINK? we have a multi-socket node and we've seen odd asymmetric perf.
[00:02:58] Samir: yes NUMA affinity plus pinned NVLINK topology can make a kernel that was fast on GPU0 slower on GPU1 because of cross-socket latency. In the traces you sent there's a pattern where kernel durations diverge right after a migration event.
[00:03:15] Priya: migration event meaning checkpointing of the KV cache?
[00:03:18] Jordan: it can be due to live migration across worker lanes when a GPU is overloaded. The runtime schedules to balance utilization which may move cached key/value shards to a different device or lane. That movement is cheap in metadata but it alters memory locality.
[00:03:33] Alex: we thought KV cache was pinned to the same worker, maybe our orchestration is moving containers. we'll check.
[00:03:40] Maya: useful, so immediate experiment set 1: disable cuda graph replay for a controlled window and compare p50/p95/p99. Jordan — you and Alex will coordinate.
[00:03:49] Jordan: yes, and also capture the graph abort stack trace on failure, that helps triage whether it's shape mismatch or a launch-time allocation failure.
[00:03:58] Priya: question — what about batching policy; we currently use a 64ms coalesce with max batch 8. should we change that?
[00:04:06] Jordan: the 64ms threshold interacts with prefix caching. For short queries the extra delay accumulates; for your workload (bimodal) one option is dynamic coalesce: use small window for short sequences and larger window for long sequences. But dynamic increases code-path complexity and can induce more kernel switching.
[00:04:24] Samir: note also that larger batching can mask cuda graph benefits but worsen latency for single user flows; there's always a latency vs throughput tradeoff.
[00:04:33] Alex: if we move to dedicated nodes (on-prem) we can tune batching per model, but we need to quantify the delta between TRT-LLM int4 and vLLM fp16. we care about both accuracy regression and tail latency.
[00:04:44] Jordan: agreed. we propose a head-to-head: same seed prompts, same hardware, run both runtime stacks with and without quantization, capture token-level timings and perplexity metrics. We'll also capture divergence in probabilities.
[00:04:57] Priya: ok how long to set that up?
[00:05:00] Jordan: 2-3 days to script and run, maybe longer if we need to repro NUMA differences.
[00:05:05] Maya: Diego — anything from security side that blocks deeper traces?
[00:05:09] Diego: we need an audit of the trace artifacts we share; no secrets in payloads, and hashed request ids only. that's fine but we need a checklist.
[00:05:18] Maya: i'll send the checklist after the call.
[00:05:21] Jordan: another interesting artifact in the logs was "kernel spin" — you can see repeated small kernel launches separated by idle microseconds — that's the runtime trying different paths and eventually choosing one. These micro-launches add up.
[00:05:35] Alex: could that be because our inference requests are coming with inconsistent max_length headers from the app?
[00:05:40] Jordan: yes header inconsistency and inconsistent session state are common real-world causes of kernel path churn. Best practice is normalize request metadata at ingress.
[00:05:48] Priya: our ingress is an internal gateway that sometimes rewrites headers; we can fix that.
[00:05:52] Samir: ok notes on cuda graphs: capture at a few sequence lengths and with/without kv cache warm. If replay fails consistently on warm cache it suggests captured shape didn't account for cached KV padding. We can also adopt capture-by-template approach: capture a few small representative shapes and choose nearest graph at runtime.
[00:06:12] Jordan: there's a cost tradeoff: more captured graphs increase memory overhead. On constrained on-prem nodes that can be non-trivial.
[00:06:20] Alex: memory overhead meaning device memory for graph nodes and temporaries?
[00:06:24] Jordan: yes, plus reserved scratch buffers. That matters when quantized kernels also have different workspace needs.
[00:06:30] Priya: what about fallback behavior — is there a way to make fallback warm quickly so replay failures don't spike p99?
[00:06:36] Jordan: one approach is shadow replay: attempt a lightweight validation instead of full replay, and if that fails, start a parallel warmup path so the app sees the non-graph path faster. This is more engineering but reduces visible tail.
[00:06:48] Maya: that sounds promising; can Redwood share a patch or config toggle?
[00:06:52] Jordan: we have an experimental flag in the runtime for shadow warmup, i'll share it but it's not GA; needs testing.
[00:06:58] Alex: ok please mark as experimental in notes.
[00:07:02] Priya: switching topic briefly: quantization parity — we've seen subtle output differences in some prompts when using int4 with TRT-LLM. is that expected?
[00:07:11] Samir: yes quantization can change logits. For most apps the delta is negligible but for high-sensitivity prompts it matters. We should run fidelity evals alongside latency runs and capture classification/QA benchmarks.
[00:07:24] Alex: is there a recommended workflow for that?
[00:07:27] Jordan: send us a few golden prompts / eval suite; we'll run both and provide a diff report: token-level probability shifts and a human-readable evaluation summary.
[00:07:36] Maya: action item — Alex to share eval suite by Friday.
[00:07:40] Alex: yep we'll do that.
[00:07:42] Priya: about on-prem networking: Diego — we saw that when a node's egress to S3 was rate-limited our gateway retried and that correlated with a tiny spike in GPU kernel start times. Could retries propagate to the runtime scheduling?
[00:07:55] Diego: retries at the app layer can cause sudden bursts of requests which yields workload skew. The kernel scheduler doesn't see network retries as different, it just sees a flurry. So mitigation is to smooth at the ingress or add backpressure so spikes are absorbed by queueing.
[00:08:10] Jordan: also consider enabling token-level streaming so long outputs flow earlier; that reduces perceived latency but doesn't change backend p99 necessarily.
[00:08:18] Alex: we do streaming for chat flows but many of these are short single-turn calls.
[00:08:22] Samir: final technical note: NVTX and detailed nvprof snapshots are super helpful. When you send traces include both kernel timeline and cuda-memcopy timeline; sometimes memcopy overlaps hide asynchrony.
[00:08:36] Jordan: ok to recap next steps: 1) disable cuda graph replay in controlled window and compare p99 (Argon+Jordan), 2) run TRT-LLM int4 vs vLLM fp16 parity and latency tests (joint), 3) KV cache stress test to force eviction and observe kernel-churn (Argon), 4) Jordan to share experimental shadow-warmup flag and capture guide, 5) Maya to send security trace-sharing checklist.
[00:08:56] Alex: sounds good. thanks, this was helpful.
[00:09:00] Maya: thanks everyone we'll follow up with a calendar for the tests and upload a benchmark template (CSV) and an nsight upload folder.
[00:09:08] Priya: thanks all.

[00:09:12] (call continues with scheduling details and brief Q&A then wraps at ~16:42 UTC)
